content_voiceover: These clinical photos show the mucocutaneous bleeding pattern typical of a platelet disorder, and they set up the case coming in the next few slides, an inherited thrombocytopenia that can mimic immune thrombocytopenic purpura. Top row: symmetric ecchymoses scattered along both forearms and dense, confluent purpura over both lower legs, exactly the small, multiple, superficial pattern the previous table told you to expect with platelet problems, in contrast to the large solitary bruises of a coagulation factor disorder. There's also a deep bruise over the upper arm and shoulder. Bottom row shows oral involvement, gingival bleeding at the gumline and a hematoma inside the cheek and oral mucosa, both classic sites for platelet-type bleeding because mucosal surfaces depend heavily on an intact platelet plug rather than the coagulation cascade. When you see this combination, spontaneous ecchymoses plus gum and mucosal bleeding, in a patient with thrombocytopenia, think platelet quantity or quality problem first, and remember that inherited causes like MYH9-related disorders can look identical to acquired ITP on exam alone.
keypoints: Multiple, small, superficial ecchymoses = platelet-type bleeding pattern
Mucosal bleeding: gingival + oral cavity = classic platelet-disorder sites
Mimics ITP clinically — inherited causes must be excluded
keypoint_voiceover: Widespread small ecchymoses on the limbs plus gingival and oral mucosal bleeding, that's the classic platelet-type bleeding pattern, mucosal and superficial rather than deep. Clinically this can look identical to immune thrombocytopenic purpura, which is exactly why inherited causes need to be ruled out before you commit to a diagnosis of ITP.
